p: Ezekiel counts the years from King Jehoiachin's exile in 597 BC; this vision comes a little over a year after his call.
b: Ezekiel dates by the years of the exile that began with Jehoiachin's deportation in 597 BC (2 Kings 24:12-16). The sixth year is 592 BC, and the sixth month, fifth day, falls in late summer (about September by the usual calculation). It is the book's second dated vision: the call came in the fifth year (1:2). The vision that follows (8:1-11:25) ends with Ezekiel telling the exiles all he saw (11:25). Four years later, in 588, Nebuchadnezzar's siege began (24:1-2; 2 Kings 25:1). Some scholars date Jerusalem's fall to 587 rather than 586 BC, which moves all these dates by a year; this site follows 586.

p: Leaders of the exile come to Ezekiel's house, as they do again at 14:1 and 20:1.
b: The exiles at Tel-abib kept their own leaders, the "elders". They come to Ezekiel's house to hear a word from the LORD (also 14:1; 20:1), and the vision falls on him while they sit there. Jeremiah wrote to "the elders of the exile" in Babylon (Jeremiah 29:1). These are the men who will learn from Ezekiel's report that the Temple they hope to return to is already unclean and about to lose the LORD's presence. Nothing in the text says they saw anything; the vision is Ezekiel's alone, and he tells them afterward (11:25).

t: Lifted by a spirit "in visions of God"
p: Was Ezekiel carried in body or only in a vision? The text says "in visions of God" and later "in the vision" (11:24).
b: Ruach can mean "spirit", "wind" or "breath"; here and at 3:12, 14 and 11:1, 24 it is a spirit that lifts and moves Ezekiel. The phrase "in visions of God" marks the journey as a vision: at the end the spirit brings him back "to the exiles in Chaldea in the vision by the spirit of God" (11:24), and in the story he never leaves his house. Whether the tour shows what was happening in the Temple, or what Ezekiel already knew of it from before 597, is a separate question (see the chapter page).

p: An image at the Temple's north gate. The word semel is rare, and what the image was is not known.
b: Semel, "image" or "statue", appears only here (8:3, 5), in 2 Chronicles 33:7, 15 and in Deuteronomy 4:16. Chronicles says Manasseh put a carved image in the house of God and later removed it. Kings says he put an Asherah pole in the Temple and that Josiah took it out (2 Kings 21:7; 23:6). Some scholars think Ezekiel means an image of that kind, brought back under Judah's last kings; others think the vision recalls Manasseh's image. The LORD calls himself a "jealous God" (Exodus 20:5; 34:14), so an image "that provokes jealousy" is a rival at his own door (Deuteronomy 32:16, 21). The Greek has a different word, "the pillar of the one who acquires".
r: 2 Chronicles 33:7; 2 Chronicles 33:15; 2 Kings 21:7; 2 Kings 23:6; Deuteronomy 4:16; Deuteronomy 32:16; Exodus 20:5

p: Ezekiel's scornful name for idols, about 39 times; it probably sounds like a word for dung.
b: Gillulim is Ezekiel's word for idols (about 39 times in the book, and only rarely outside it: about nine times, for example Leviticus 26:30 and Deuteronomy 29:17). Its sound suggests gelel, "dung pellets", so it is probably an insult, in the way that some writers turn the name Baal into bosheth, "shame". Some dictionaries derive it instead from galal, "roll", for rolled or round blocks of stone. The Greek has simply eidola, "idols". The Plain says "filthy idols" every time. Do not confuse it with shiqqutsim "detestable things" or to'evot "abhorrent things" (8:6): the three words overlap but are not the same.

a: every form of crawling creature and beast
p: Carved animals and "crawling creatures": scholars compare Egyptian animal cults, but the Hebrew names no god.
b: Leviticus 11 calls small swarming and crawling creatures detestable (Leviticus 11:41-43), and Deuteronomy 4:16-18 forbids an image of any animal or creeping thing. Ezekiel names no god. Judah's last kings leaned on Egypt (Pharaoh Necho made Jehoiakim king, 2 Kings 23:34), so some interpreters think of Egyptian animal cults; others think of animal figures in Mesopotamian temple art. None of these is certain. Ezekiel stresses the place: a whole hidden room of engraved images, "all around", inside the Temple precinct.

p: Shaphan was Josiah's secretary, and his family later backed Jeremiah. His son stands among the idolaters.
b: Shaphan the secretary read the found law book to King Josiah (2 Kings 22:3-13). His sons and grandson later protected Jeremiah (Jeremiah 26:24; 36:10-12; 29:3; 39:14). A son named Jaazaniah standing in the middle of the seventy elders, with a censer, shows how far Josiah's reform had been undone: leaders of the house of Israel are doing this, not only the rabble. A different Jaazaniah, son of Azzur, appears at 11:1. The Greek (Codex Vaticanus) has "Jechonias" here, perhaps through confusion with the king's other name, Jeconiah.

a: The LORD does not see us. The LORD has left the land.
p: The elders' saying that God has abandoned the land; the next chapters answer it by showing he sees, and will leave.
b: The elders' words are the people's own explanation of 597 BC: the LORD has left the land, so he can neither see nor act. The same saying is quoted again at 9:9. It echoes the wicked man's "The LORD does not see" (Psalm 94:7; Psalm 10:11; Isaiah 29:15) and Jeremiah's answer that no one can hide in secret places where the LORD does not see (Jeremiah 23:24). The vision turns the claim around: the LORD sees everything done in the dark, and chapters 10-11 show that he will indeed leave, but because of what they do, not because he is blind.

p: The Mesopotamian god of the dying summer vegetation, mourned by women each year; this verse is the Bible's only mention.
b: Tammuz is the Babylonian form of the Sumerian Dumuzi, the shepherd-god whom the goddess Inanna (Ishtar) sent to the underworld in her place. Women mourned him each midsummer, when the grass withered, and the Hebrew month Tammuz (June-July) is named after him. The Greek has Thammouz, and Jerome (Commentary on Ezekiel) identifies him with Adonis, whose Greek cult was similar. This verse is the only evidence that the rite was held at the Temple. Whether it was a widespread women's custom or Ezekiel chose its most shocking form is debated. For women's devotion to another deity see Jeremiah 44:15-19.

a: bowing low to the sun in the east
t: Sun worship at the Temple door
p: The Temple faced east, so men bowing to the rising sun turn their backs on the LORD's house.
b: The LORD's Temple opened to the east, so men with their backs to it and their faces east were bowing to the rising sun. The Torah forbids bowing to the sun, moon or stars (Deuteronomy 4:19; 17:3), and Josiah had removed from the Temple entrance the horses and chariots earlier kings had dedicated to the sun (2 Kings 23:5, 11). The Mishnah (Sukkah 5:4) quotes this verse in the Sukkot ceremony: those who reached the Temple's east gate turned toward the Temple and said that their fathers had done this, but that they themselves looked to the LORD. Some scholars think the Judean sun cult began as worship of the LORD under a solar image; the verse treats it as a rival.

t: "They send the branch to their nose"
p: A puzzling gesture. Some lists of scribal corrections are said to include this verse, and the Greek reads differently.
b: Zemorah, a "branch" or "vine shoot", appears elsewhere in Numbers 13:23 and Isaiah 17:10. The gesture is not explained. Proposals: a rite of worship, an insult toward the LORD, or a vulgar gesture. Some medieval lists of the "scribal corrections" (tiqqune soferim), where scribes were said to have softened language about God, are reported to include this verse, with the original reading "my nose" (see McCarthy's study of the corrections); the evidence is uncertain. Codex Vaticanus has "like people sneering" instead of the branch (see the variant). The Plain follows the Hebrew and leaves the meaning open.

a: they are sending me far from my sanctuary
t: Driven far from his own house
p: The people's sins push the LORD away from his Temple. Chapters 10-11 show him going.
b: The Hebrew says the sins are "to be far from on my sanctuary": their effect is to put distance between the LORD and his house. The Plain makes the cause explicit ("sending me far"). The word "far" returns in 11:15-16, where Jerusalem says the exiles are "far from the LORD" while the LORD says he scattered them far and is still a little sanctuary to them. The abhorrent things (to'evot) of this verse are one of three words for idol-worship; see the note at 5:11.

a: The punishments of the city have come near
p: The Hebrew word can mean punishments or those appointed over the city; the vowel marks give the first.
b: Pequddot is from paqad, "visit, attend to", and can mean "visitations" (punishments, as in Isaiah 10:3) or "those appointed" (overseers, as in 2 Kings 11:18). The verb qarvu is read in the Masoretic vowel marks as "have come near". With other vowels it is a command, qirvu: "Come near, you who are in charge of the city!", which would fit the six men arriving in the next verse. The Greek has "the punishment of the city has drawn near". The Plain follows the vowel marks; either way the six men come as the LORD's agents.

a: One man among them was clothed in linen
t: The six and the man in linen
p: Seven heavenly figures; the one in linen carries a scribe's case. Jewish and Christian readers name him differently.
b: The six carry weapons; the seventh, dressed in linen, carries writing tools. Ezekiel does not call any of them angels, but the later Bible does for a "man clothed in linen" (Daniel 10:5; 12:6-7; compare the seven angels of Tobit 12:15 and Revelation 8:2). Linen is also the clothing of priests (Leviticus 16:4). The Talmud names him Gabriel (Shabbat 55a). Ezekiel gives no name, and the story does not depend on one.
r: Daniel 10:5; Daniel 12:6-7; Tobit 12:15; Revelation 8:2; Revelation 15:6; Leviticus 16:4

a: The glory of the God of Israel went up
t: The first step of the glory's departure
p: The glory, last seen over the cherub in the Holy of Holies, moves to the threshold. It leaves in stages.
b: Kavod, "glory", is the visible presence of the LORD, seen at Sinai and in the wilderness tent (Exodus 24:16-17; 40:34-35) and filling Solomon's Temple (1 Kings 8:10-11). In 9:3 it leaves its place on the cherub in the Holy of Holies and moves to the threshold. It leaves in stages: the threshold (9:3; 10:4), the east gate (10:18-19) and the mountain east of the city (11:22-23). Jewish tradition counted "ten journeys" of the divine Presence from the Temple to heaven (Rosh Hashanah 31a). Josephus tells of the Temple's inner east gate swinging open by itself at night, and of a voice saying "Let us depart from here", in the years before the Romans took the city (Jewish War 6.5.3). The glory returns in 43:1-5.

p: Here the Hebrew has one cherub; chapter 10 says the living creatures of chapter 1 were cherubim.
b: The Hebrew has the singular "the cherub" here (the Greek has the plural, "the cherubim"). The Ark's lid carried two golden cherubim, and the LORD is said to sit "above the cherubim" (1 Samuel 4:4; Psalm 99:1), so the cherub here is the throne-bearer of the Holy of Holies. In chapter 10 Ezekiel says that the creatures he saw by the Kebar were cherubim (10:15, 20); chapter 1 had called them "living creatures". The note at 10:14 explains why one face changes from ox to cherub.

p: The Hebrew word is the name of the last letter, tav. In the old script it looked like a cross.
b: The Hebrew word is tav, the last letter of the alphabet. In the old Hebrew script that Ezekiel's readers used, the letter was a cross-shaped sign (a plus or an X); the square script came later. Christian writers saw a cross here: Origen, Tertullian and Jerome are among those who say so (reported by Jerome in his commentary). Rashi says the sign was set on the foreheads of the righteous so that the destroyers would not strike them. The Talmud has Gabriel write the tav in ink on the righteous and in blood on the wicked, and explains it as tihyeh, "you will live", and tamut, "you will die" (Shabbat 55a). A mark that spares recalls the blood on the doorposts of Passover (Exodus 12:7, 13), and it is the pattern for the seal on the foreheads of God's servants in Revelation 7:3 and 9:4.

p: Judgment starts with the Temple and its elders, the people who knew the most.
b: The killing starts with "the old men who were in front of the house", the leaders of 8:11, 16. The principle is that those closest to the LORD are judged first (Amos 3:2; Jeremiah 25:29). The New Testament applies it to the church: judgment begins with the household of God (1 Peter 4:17). In the chapter, the sparing mark goes to people who grieve over the sin; the verse does not say that they were sinless, only that they refused to join.

p: The LORD orders corpses in his own courts. A dead body made a place unclean, so he is giving up his house.
b: A dead body made a person or place ritually unclean (Numbers 19:11-13), and the priests were kept from the dead (Leviticus 21:1-4). Filling the courts with corpses is therefore the opposite of a cleansing: the LORD himself makes his house unfit to live in. This prepares for the glory's departure in the next two chapters. The killers are not men of Israel; they are agents from the LORD's heavenly council. The passage is not a command for people to kill, and no later text takes it that way.

p: Ezekiel pleads as Moses and Amos did. The LORD's answer is that the guilt is too great.
b: Ezekiel falls on his face and pleads, as Abraham did for Sodom (Genesis 18:23-25), Moses after the golden calf (Exodus 32:11-13) and Amos for Jacob (Amos 7:2, 5). He repeats the cry at 11:13. The LORD's answer is not to refuse mercy in principle but to say that this generation's guilt is beyond what prayer can turn (9:9-10). Later he says that even Noah, Daniel and Job would save only themselves (14:14, 20), and he told Jeremiah not to pray for this people (Jeremiah 7:16).

p: Two charges: blood spilled (dam) and twisted justice (mutteh). The Greek has "uncleanness" for the second.
b: Dam ("blood") here means the shedding of innocent blood; Ezekiel calls Jerusalem "the city of bloodshed" at 22:2 and 24:6, 9. Mutteh is a rare word, from natah, "bend", and the context suggests justice turned crooked. The Greek has akatharsia, "uncleanness", which may reflect a different reading or a guess. The quotation "The LORD has left the land" repeats the saying of 8:12, with "does not see" now added. The guilt is both moral and religious: crimes against people and idols in the Temple.

t: Fire from the throne for the city
p: Coals from between the cherubim are to be sprinkled over Jerusalem. The story never says it happened.
b: In Isaiah 6:6-7 a seraph takes a coal from the altar and touches Isaiah's lips to cleanse him. Here the coals from the throne are for the city, and the verb is zaraq, "sprinkle" or "dash" (the word for dashing blood on the altar and for Moses tossing ashes in Exodus 9:8; seed and chaff are scattered with a different verb), so that the fire is flung over the whole city. The narrative never says the man sprinkled them; it only says he took the coals and went out (10:7). The reader is left with the fire in his hands. Fulfillment in history came when the Babylonians burned the Temple and city (2 Kings 25:9). In Revelation 8:5 an angel fills his censer with altar fire and throws it to the earth, a close echo.

p: The cloud that filled Solomon's Temple at its dedication now fills the court before the glory leaves.
b: When the tent in the wilderness was finished, the cloud covered it and the glory of the LORD filled it (Exodus 40:34-35). In Solomon's day the cloud filled the house and the priests could not stand to serve (1 Kings 8:10-11). In Ezekiel the same signs return, but now they show the presence on the point of leaving. The cloud and the brightness are the glory's outward form, not the glory itself, and the next verses show it move.

p: The traditional English for an old name of God whose meaning is uncertain. Ezekiel uses it here and at 1:24.
b: El Shaddai is the name by which God was known to the patriarchs (Genesis 17:1; Exodus 6:3). The Greek tradition said "Almighty" (pantokrator), and the English tradition followed. Its origin is uncertain: "mountain", "breast" and "destroyer" have all been proposed. Ezekiel uses it only for the sound of the creatures' wings (1:24; 10:5), like the sound of thunder or an army. The Plain keeps "God Almighty", because that is the name's long English use, and leaves the origin open. The Greek here keeps the name as a transliteration, Saddai.

p: A second Hebrew word for wheel, used only here in the vision. The Greek turns it into a name, "Gelgel".
b: Galgal is not the ordinary word for wheel (ofan, used elsewhere in chapters 1 and 10). It means something that rolls or whirls, as in the "wheels" of a chariot in Isaiah 5:28 or the "whirlwind" of Psalm 77:18. The text says the wheels were "called" this "in my hearing", so it may be a title shouted over them. The Greek treats galgal as a proper name, Gelgel. Scholars suggest it names a whirling wheelwork that rolled with the throne-chariot. The Plain keeps both words apart: "wheels" for ofannim and "whirling wheel" for galgal.

p: Chapter 1 gives the first face as an ox; here it is a cherub. Rabbis and scholars explain the change differently.
b: See also the note at 1:10. In 1:10 the four faces are a human's, a lion's, an ox's and an eagle's. Here the ox has become "a cherub". Explanations: (1) The Talmud says that Ezekiel pleaded and the ox face was changed to a cherub so that Israel's accuser could not point to the golden calf (Hagigah 13b). (2) A cherub in the ancient Near East was a winged guardian often shown with a bull's body, so "the face of the cherub" may simply be the bull-face under another name. (3) The Hebrew text has been disturbed. Codex Vaticanus has no text at 10:14 at all (see the variant). In 41:18-19 the Temple's carved cherubim have two faces, a man and a lion.

a: the spirit of the living creature
p: The same words as 1:20-21. The wheels rise and stop with the creatures because their spirit is in them.
b: Ruach may be "spirit", "breath" or "wind". In 1:20-21 the creatures go "wherever the spirit would go", and "the spirit of the living creature was in the wheels". Here the same phrase says the wheels move together with the cherubim because the creature's single driving force is in them. Some scholars read "spirit" as the will that moves the whole chariot; some read "the spirit of life", as the Greek does (pneuma zoes). The Plain says "spirit", because the same Hebrew word returns in 11:1 and 11:5 for the spirit that moves Ezekiel.

a: the entrance of the east gate
p: The glory pauses at the gate facing the Mount of Olives. In 43:1-5 it returns through the same gate.
b: The Temple faced east, and the east gate of the house of the LORD is the way out toward the Kidron valley and the Mount of Olives. The glory stops there, ready to cross, and in 11:23 it leaves the city. In the vision of the future Temple, the glory of the LORD comes into the house by the gate that faces east (43:4), and the gate is then shut (44:1-2). Josephus tells that before AD 70 the Temple's east gate swung open by itself at night (Jewish War 6.5.3).

a: I knew that they were cherubim
p: In chapter 1 Ezekiel called them "living creatures". Now, at the Temple, he knows what they are.
b: In chapter 1 the creatures had no name. In the Temple Ezekiel recognizes them: they are the cherubim of the Holy of Holies, the guardians of the Ark's lid (Exodus 25:18-22) and the carved figures on the Temple walls and doors (1 Kings 6:23-35). This verse is the key that joins his call-vision to the Temple, and it is why Jewish and Christian tradition call chapter 1 the vision of the "chariot" (merkavah), with the cherubim as its throne-bearers. The Hebrew of 10:15 says "the living creature" in the singular, as a collective.

p: The Hebrew says four wings each, as in chapter 1. Codex Vaticanus says eight.
b: The Hebrew has "four wings" for each cherub, matching 1:6. Codex Vaticanus, as printed by Swete, reads "eight wings", as if each creature had twice the wings; the reason is unknown. 4QEzek-a (4Q73) preserves this verse and agrees with the Masoretic Text apart from writing the number "four" in its masculine form before "wings" (a spelling and grammar difference that does not change the sense).

a: Jaazaniah son of Azzur and Pelatiah son of Benaiah
t: Two officials at the east gate
p: Not the Jaazaniah of 8:11. These men are "officials of the people" at the gate where the glory is about to leave.
b: The east gate is where the glory stopped in 10:19, and these twenty-five men are in its entrance. The Jaazaniah here is the son of Azzur, a different man from Jaazaniah son of Shaphan (8:11). The Hebrew word for "officials" (sarim) is the ordinary word for royal and city officers, not nasi, "leader". Codex Vaticanus gives the first man as "Jechonias son of Ezer" and spells Pelatiah "Phaltias". The text does not say whether they are the same twenty-five as the sun-worshipers of 8:16; the number matches, but the Hebrew places them elsewhere.

a: The time to build houses is not near
t: A hard saying about building houses
p: A line that is hard in Hebrew; it has been read as a statement, a question and as something else in the Greek.
b: Lo be-qarov benot batim is literally "not near the building of houses". Readings: (1) A statement, "the time to build houses is not near", meaning either that no disaster is near and rebuilding is not needed, or that nothing is worth building now. (2) A question, "Is it not near, the building of houses?", meaning "Let us build", a boast of security like the opposite of Jeremiah's advice to build houses in exile (Jeremiah 29:5). (3) The Greek reads "Have not the houses been built recently?" (Codex Vaticanus, in Swete), a different division of the words. Commentators lean to different readings, and all agree that the speakers feel safe inside Jerusalem.
orig: לֹא בְקָרוֹב בְּנוֹת בָּתִּים (lo beqarov benot battim)

a: This city is the pot, and we are the meat
p: Leaders boast that the city's walls protect them as a pot protects meat from the fire. Ezekiel reverses it.
b: The saying means: Jerusalem's walls shelter us, as a cooking pot holds the meat, so we will not be burned. Ezekiel takes the picture and turns it. The "meat" is the slain they have put in the city, and the people themselves will be taken out of the pot (11:7, 9, 11). He returns to the pot with a full parable in 24:3-14, and in Jeremiah 1:13 the boiling pot is the image of the northern invasion. The idea that the city is a safe container for its leaders is the same confidence as "The LORD's temple" in Jeremiah 7:4.

a: Then you will know that I am the LORD
t: "Then you will know that I am the LORD"
p: Ezekiel's recognition formula. In chapters 8-15 it closes judgments and promises alike.
b: The refrain is explained at 5:13. In chapters 8-15 it closes 11 verses: 11:10, 12; 12:15, 16, 20; 13:9, 14, 21, 23; 14:8; 15:7 (counted in this Plain). The Plain keeps one English sentence each time, and in 13:9 the Hebrew has the longer name, "the Lord GOD". The knowledge the refrain promises usually comes through judgment: Israel learns who the LORD is by what he does. In 11:10-12 the leaders who say the city is a pot learn it by falling at the border.
orig: וִידַעְתֶּם כִּי אֲנִי יְהוָה (vida'tem ki ani YHWH)

p: A man dies as Ezekiel prophesies, and he cries out again, as he did in 9:8.
b: Pelatiah is one of the two leaders named in 11:1. His death comes while Ezekiel speaks, which shows that the word is true. The story is told inside the vision, so it may be a vision of a death rather than a death reported from Jerusalem. Jeremiah's word that the false prophet Hananiah would die within the year, and his death two months later, is the nearest parallel (Jeremiah 28:15-17). Ezekiel responds as he did in 9:8: he falls on his face and asks whether the LORD will make a full end of the remnant.

p: A strange Hebrew phrase. The Greek reads "the men of your exile", which makes simple sense.
b: Ge'ullah is the duty of a close relative to redeem a family member or family land (Leviticus 25:25-28; Ruth 3-4). "The men of your redemption" would then be Ezekiel's kinsmen, who with him share the exile. The Greek (Codex Vaticanus) has "men of your captivity", reading galut, "exile", for ge'ullah, and it fits the context of the exiles. The Plain keeps the Hebrew and lets the gloss explain it. The charge is clear in either reading: Jerusalem's people called the exiles "far from the LORD" and claimed the land as their own.

p: The Hebrew can mean a small sanctuary, a sanctuary for a little while, or a sanctuary in small measure.
b: Miqdash me'at has three readings: (1) "a small sanctuary": the LORD himself is the exiles' Temple, in a small way; (2) "a sanctuary for a little while", until the return of 11:17; (3) "to some extent", a sanctuary in part. The Talmud takes it as the synagogues and houses of study in Babylon (Megillah 29a). The Greek has "a small holy place" (hagiasma mikron). The verse is the first sign that the LORD can be present among his people without the Temple, a thought fuller in chapters 40-48 and in the New Testament sense of the body of believers as a temple (1 Corinthians 3:16).

p: A second word for idols, less often used than gillulim. The Greek does not tell the three words apart.
b: Shiqqutsim ("detestable things") is a word for idols or idol-related objects (Deuteronomy 29:17; 2 Kings 23:13, 24). Ezekiel uses it about eight times and joins it here with to'evot, "abhorrent things" (see 8:6). The third word, gillulim, "filthy idols", is explained at 8:10. The Greek uses bdelygmata and anomiai in this verse and does not keep the three apart. The Plain keeps the three Hebrew words separate so that the reader can tell which one Ezekiel chose.

p: The Hebrew says one heart, undivided. The Greek has another heart, and Ezekiel 36:26 has a new one.
b: The Hebrew says lev echad, "one heart", a heart not divided between the LORD and idols. Jeremiah 32:39 has the same phrase in a similar promise of one heart and one way, and Psalm 86:11 prays for a united heart. The Greek (Codex Vaticanus) reads "another heart" (kardian heteran), which fits "new spirit" and Ezekiel 36:26, "a new heart". The Plain keeps the Masoretic Text, which has support in Jeremiah 32:39. See the variant.

t: The new spirit and the heart of flesh
p: God gives a new spirit and replaces a stone heart with a heart of flesh. 36:26-27 repeats it almost word for word.
b: The heart in Hebrew is the center of thought, will and feeling, and "stone" and "flesh" mean unresponsive and responsive. Ezekiel 36:26-27 repeats the promise with "heart" and "spirit" both new, and adds "my Spirit". In 18:31 the LORD tells Israel to "make yourselves a new heart and a new spirit", so the new heart is both a command and a promise. Ruach ("spirit") here is the person's inner life, not yet the LORD's own Spirit; the move from one to the other is the work of chapter 36. Jeremiah 31:33 promises the Law written on the heart, which is the same hope in other words. The Hebrew shifts person inside the verse: "I will give them one heart" and then "a new spirit inside you"; the Plain keeps the shift. In 11:5 the same word ruach is rendered "mind" (what comes up in the spirit).

a: my people, and I will be their God
p: "They will be my people, and I will be their God" appears throughout the Bible.
b: The sentence is the shortest form of the covenant, that God will be Israel's God and Israel his people (Leviticus 26:12; Exodus 6:7; Jeremiah 31:33). Ezekiel uses it at 14:11; 36:28; 37:23, 27. Revelation 21:3 turns the promise toward the end of time, when God lives with his people. Here the sentence comes right after the promise of a new heart and obedience, so the covenant is renewed by what God does, not by what Israel promises.

a: stood on the mountain east of the city
t: The mountain east of the city
p: The glory halts on the Mount of Olives, not named here. Later texts link it to the return of God's presence.
b: The "mountain east of the city" is the Mount of Olives, across the Kidron valley. Jewish tradition says the Presence waited there three and a half years, calling Israel to return, before it went up to heaven (Rosh Hashanah 31a). In Zechariah 14:4 the LORD stands on the Mount of Olives on the day of his coming. In the New Testament Jesus ascends from the Mount of Olives (Acts 1:9-12), and the angels say he will come back the same way; Christian writers have connected the two scenes. In 43:1-5 the glory returns from the east.

a: They have eyes to see but do not see
p: The same charge as Isaiah, Jeremiah and Moses. For the name "rebellious house" see the note at 2:5.
b: The charge that the people have eyes and ears and do not use them is old. Moses said the LORD had not yet given Israel a heart to know, eyes to see or ears to hear (Deuteronomy 29:4). Isaiah was sent to a people who would hear and not understand (Isaiah 6:9-10), and Jeremiah called them foolish people who have eyes and do not see (Jeremiah 5:21). Ezekiel is told the same of the "rebellious house" (see 2:5). The sign act that follows is meant to be seen: it is the LORD's way of getting through to people who do not look.

a: pack an exile's baggage for yourself
p: Ezekiel acts out the coming exile in daylight, as the exiles watch. The sign is a public performance.
b: The first sign acts (chapters 4-5) showed the siege; this one shows the flight (whether such acts were performed or only told is discussed at 4:3). Ezekiel's baggage is what an exile could carry: a bundle, a bowl, a cloak. The sign is a mofet, a portent (12:6, 11; 24:24, 27). The word "perhaps" (ulai) shows the sign aims to be understood, even though the audience has not understood before. Other prophets acted signs too (Isaiah 20; Jeremiah 13; 19; 27).

p: A heading for a prophetic burden. In Ezekiel it appears as a title only here.
b: Massa' comes from nasa', "lift up", and means a "lifting up" of the voice or a load; the KJV says "burden". It heads oracles in Isaiah 13-23 and Zechariah 9, 12 and Malachi. In Ezekiel it appears as a prophetic title only here; the Plain says "oracle", as elsewhere on this site. Codex Vaticanus does not translate the word and reads "the ruler and the leader in Jerusalem". The sense is that this sign act, like a prophet's oracle, is addressed to a particular person, the king in Jerusalem.

p: The KJV and many versions say "prince". This Plain says "leader" for the Hebrew nasi, here King Zedekiah.
b: Nasi, from nasa' "lift up", is a person raised up as head of a tribe or a nation (Genesis 17:20; Numbers 7). The KJV and many other versions say "prince", which in English suggests a king's son; Ezekiel uses nasi for the reigning king Zedekiah here, for Judah's kings in 19:1 and 21:25, and later for the ideal head of the restored people (34:24; 37:25; 44:3; 45:7-22). Ezekiel does use "king" (melekh) at times (17:12; 37:22, 24), but nasi is his usual word for Israel's own head, and why is debated; one view is that it stresses the ruler's place under the LORD.

p: The riddle: Ezekiel says Zedekiah will not see Babylon but will die there. 2 Kings 25 and Jeremiah 52 tell how.
b: In 586 BC, when the walls were broken, Zedekiah left the city by night through the gate between the two walls, but the Babylonians caught him near Jericho, took him to Riblah, killed his sons before him, put out his eyes, and took him in chains to Babylon (2 Kings 25:4-7; Jeremiah 39:4-7; 52:7-11). Jeremiah 52:11 says he died in prison there. So both Jeremiah's word that Zedekiah would see the king of Babylon (Jeremiah 34:3) and Ezekiel's that he would not see Babylon came true. Josephus says that Zedekiah thought the two prophecies contradicted each other and so believed neither (Jewish Antiquities 10.6.3, §§106-107). The blinding and capture themselves are told in 10.7.2, §§141-142.

a: I will leave a few of them alive
p: A few are spared so that they can tell the nations why. The survivors become witnesses, not just survivors.
b: The remnant has a job: to "tell about all their abhorrent things among the nations" so that the nations too will know why the exile happened. The same idea is found in 6:8-10 and 14:22-23, where the survivors' evil ways convince Ezekiel's hearers that God was right to judge. In Lamentations and Psalm 79 the survivors pray rather than recount. In Isaiah 66:19 survivors are sent to the nations to declare the LORD's glory. The idea in Ezekiel is that the exile will carry a message to the world about the LORD's justice.

p: A phrase that names different groups in different places. Here it probably means the exiles.
b: See the note at 7:27 for the term. Here it probably names the whole community in Babylon, to whom Ezekiel is told to speak about those left in Jerusalem. Elsewhere the same phrase names the landowning citizens who put Josiah on the throne (2 Kings 21:24; 23:30) or the ordinary population (Jeremiah 34:19). The Plain always says "the people of the land" and lets the context decide.

p: A saying people repeated. Ezekiel quotes it and tells them it will stop.
b: Mashal can mean "proverb", "saying", "parable" or "riddle", depending on the context. In 12:22-23 it is a quoted saying that people say among themselves; in 17:2 it is a "riddle and parable" (chidah and mashal); in 18:2-3 it is another quoted proverb ("The fathers ate sour grapes..."). The Plain uses "proverb" when the people are quoting something, and "parable" when Ezekiel tells a story. The saying here, "The days drag on, and every vision fails", is the mood of the exiles in 592 BC: the earlier warnings had not come true, so it was easy to assume they never would.

p: The people say prophecy is slow; the LORD says it is near. The complaint reappears in other books.
b: The complaint "the days drag on" is old and keeps returning. Isaiah's hearers dared the LORD to hurry and finish his work (Isaiah 5:19). Jeremiah's hearers asked where the word of the LORD was and told it to come (Jeremiah 17:15). Habakkuk was told that if the vision seems slow he should wait for it (Habakkuk 2:3). Centuries later, scoffers in the church asked what had become of the promise of Christ's coming (2 Peter 3:3-4), and the answer there is that the Lord is patient (2 Peter 3:8-9). Ezekiel's answer is the shortest: it will not be put off. Six years later Jerusalem fell.

p: Two names for false prophecy. The next chapter takes them up.
b: Chazon shav', "empty vision", is a vision with nothing in it; miqsam chalaq, "smooth divination", is a prediction that flatters. Both are the work of the prophets whom Ezekiel attacks in chapter 13, who say what people want to hear. Jeremiah makes the same charge: they treat the people's wound lightly and say there is peace when there is none (Jeremiah 6:14; 23:16-17). Lamentations 2:14 says the prophets saw empty and false visions and so did not expose Israel's guilt. The test in Deuteronomy 18:20-22 is whether the word comes true.
orig: חֲזוֹן שָׁוְא ... מִקְסַם חָלָק (chazon shav' ... miqsam chalaq)

t: Whom Ezekiel is told to answer
p: Prophets in Jerusalem and in Babylon were saying that the exile would end soon.
b: Ezekiel's rivals were not only in Jerusalem. Jeremiah's letter to the exiles warns against prophets in Babylon who said the exile was short (Jeremiah 29:8-9, 21-23), and Hananiah in Jerusalem had said in the temple that the yoke of Babylon would be broken within two years (Jeremiah 28:1-4). Ezekiel does not name any. His test is the one in the next verses: they prophesy "out of their own hearts", they say the LORD declares when he has not sent them, and their "peace" has no ground. Deuteronomy 18:20-22 sets the same marks: a prophet who speaks what the LORD did not command, or whose word does not come true, is false.

p: A cry from funerals, used by the prophets to announce that a group is already as good as dead.
b: Hoy is the cry of mourners at a funeral (1 Kings 13:30, where a prophet is mourned). The prophets use it before the people they are condemning, as if the funeral were already being held (Isaiah 5:8-23; Amos 5:18). In this Plain it is "Woe to" before a group, "Alas" at a funeral, and "Hey!" for a bare call. Ezekiel uses hoy only a few times, for example here, at 13:18, at 24:6, 9 (the city of bloodshed) and at 34:2 (the shepherds). Each time it announces a doom on those who should have protected the people.

p: Animals that live in broken places and profit from them, but never mend a wall.
b: Shu'al can mean fox or jackal, small animals that den in ruins and scavenge (Lamentations 5:18; Nehemiah 4:3, where one fox could break a wall). The prophets are like them: they live in the broken city, take what they can get, and do nothing to repair it. The next verse says what they failed to do, which is to build the wall that would hold in battle. The Greek has "foxes in the deserts". The Plain says "foxes" and lets the image of ruins stand.

a: on the day of the LORD
t: The breach, the wall and the day of the LORD
p: A true prophet stands in the gap and pleads or warns. These prophets did neither.
b: A breach is a gap in a city wall where an enemy comes through. In Israel's memory Moses had "stood in the breach" to turn God's anger from the people (Psalm 106:23), and in 22:30 the LORD searches for someone to do the same and finds no one. The prophets of chapter 13 could have repaired the people's walls by calling them to turn back. Instead they plastered over the cracks (13:10). "The day of the LORD" is the day of reckoning (Amos 5:18-20; Zephaniah 1:14-16); here it is the day Babylon's army would come.

a: written in the register of the house of Israel
p: No seat in the council, no name in the register, no return to the land.
b: The three losses grow more serious. "The council of my people" is their assembly. The "register" is the written roll of the citizens, as in Ezra 2:62 and Nehemiah 7:5, where those not listed could not serve as priests; it echoes the book of life in Exodus 32:32 and Daniel 12:1. And not entering "the land of Israel" means no part in the return of which Ezekiel will speak (11:17; 20:34-42; 34:13). The false prophets promised peace to the whole people; they themselves will have no share in what comes.

a: Then you will know that I am the Lord GOD
t: "The Lord GOD" in the recognition formula
p: Most often the sentence says "the LORD"; five times in Ezekiel it says "the Lord GOD".
b: The recognition formula usually ends "you will know that I am the LORD" (11:10, 12; 12:15-16, 20; 13:14, 21, 23). Here it ends with the longer name, Adonai YHWH, "the Lord GOD". The same long form occurs at 23:49; 24:24; 28:24 and 29:16. Each time the verse is about a recognition that comes through judgment on a particular group. The Plain keeps the difference so that the reader can see it; the Greek has "I am the Lord" in all these places.
orig: כִּי אֲנִי אֲדֹנָי יְהוִה (ki ani Adonai YHWH)

t: Tafel: whitewash on a weak wall
p: The Hebrew word suggests something flimsy or tasteless. The image is a wall that looks solid but is not.
b: Tafel appears in 13:10-15 and 22:28. The related adjective means "tasteless", as in Job 6:6 (food without salt). The word probably means a coating of plaster or lime that looks like finish but adds no strength. The KJV says "untempered morter"; the Greek has aloiphe, "plaster". The picture is of a rough wall of loose stones that someone has covered to look strong. Some scholars think the wall is the people's policy of resisting Babylon with help from Egypt (17:15), and that the prophets covered it with words of peace. Others take it as an everyday image with no particular policy.

p: The false prophets' one word. Jeremiah's hearers heard it from the same kind of voices.
b: Shalom, "peace", is the word the false prophets used for every danger. Jeremiah quotes the same cry: they treat the people's wound lightly, saying "Peace, peace" when there is no peace (Jeremiah 6:14; 8:11), and they tell those who despise the LORD that no harm will come (Jeremiah 23:17). Micah says prophets cry "peace" for those who feed them (Micah 3:5). Ezekiel's word picture is that a wall, however well plastered, will not stand against a flood. Jesus used a related picture of a house built on sand (Matthew 7:24-27), and Paul called the high priest a "whitewashed wall" (Acts 23:3).
r: Jeremiah 6:14; Jeremiah 8:11; Jeremiah 23:17; Micah 3:5; Matthew 7:24-27; Acts 23:3

p: The LORD's storm tears the wall down. Isaiah used the same picture of a refuge of lies.
b: A storm is the LORD's usual weapon against what people trust. Isaiah 28:15-17 says the leaders of Jerusalem made lies their refuge, and hail would sweep it away and water flood the hiding place. Ezekiel gives the picture three storm forces: rain that floods, hail that batters, wind that breaks through. In 38:22 the same three come against Gog. The Hebrew addresses the hailstones directly ("you, hailstones"), as if they were being called to their task.

a: the daughters of your people who prophesy
p: Ezekiel does not object that these are women, but that they prophesy out of their own hearts.
b: The Bible names women prophets with no hint of criticism: Miriam (Exodus 15:20), Deborah (Judges 4:4), Huldah (2 Kings 22:14), and in the New Testament Anna (Luke 2:36) and Philip's daughters (Acts 21:9). Ezekiel's charge against these women is the charge against the men in 13:2: they prophesy "out of their own hearts". In Nehemiah 6:14 a prophetess, Noadiah, is also named among those who tried to frighten him. What is condemned is the practice, not the sex of the people who practise it. Whether these women were Israelite diviners in Babylon or in Jerusalem is not stated.

p: Two rare words for the women's tools. Their exact use is not known, though they look like magic.
b: Kesatot ("bands") occurs only in 13:18, 20, and mispachot ("long veils") only in 13:18, 21. The Greek has "pillows" for the first and "coverings" for the second. The picture is of women who tie something on the wrists or joints of their clients and drape veils over heads of every height, to "hunt lives", which seems to mean casting spells that bind and kill or release and spare. Scholars compare Mesopotamian magic that used knots, bands and cloths, but the practice here is not known. The Hebrew says "my hands", probably a copying slip for "their hands" (see the variant). The end of 13:20 is also unclear: the Hebrew can mean "like birds" or "to make them fly".

a: a few handfuls of barley and scraps of bread
p: The charge is that they sold false words for the cheapest pay. Micah 3:5 says the same of prophets.
b: A handful of barley and a piece of bread is the lowest pay possible. The charge matches Micah 3:5, where prophets "cry peace" for the one who feeds them and "declare war" on the one who does not. It also fits Ezekiel's larger charge that those who profit from their words "profane" the LORD to his own people. Their victims are those they sentence to die or promise to keep alive without the LORD's word. The rule behind it is in Deuteronomy 18:20 and Jeremiah 14:14-15.

a: so that he does not turn from his evil way
t: Comfort for the wicked, grief for the righteous
p: A false word makes the righteous sad and the wicked sure. It stops the wicked from turning back.
b: The lie cuts both ways. It saddens the righteous, who are told that the LORD will not act, and it supports the wicked, who feel safe and do not repent. Jeremiah says the same: the prophets strengthen evildoers so that no one turns from wickedness (Jeremiah 23:14). Ezekiel's concern is that the wicked should turn and live; that is the center of chapter 18, 33:11-20, and the LORD's own pleasure in life (18:23, 32). The false prophet takes away that door.

a: brought their filthy idols up into their hearts
p: These elders may have no idol in sight. The idols are in their hearts, and the Greek reads "thoughts".
b: Ezekiel's word for idols, gillulim, is here set "in the heart". The picture is that of a person who comes to ask the LORD while holding something else in the center of his will. The "stumbling block of guilt" (mikhshol 'avon) is whatever trips a person into sin (7:19; 18:30; 44:12). The Greek has "thoughts" and "punishment" for the two nouns. Calvin's saying that the human mind is a "perpetual factory of idols" (Institutes 1.11.8) is often applied to this verse, though he does not discuss Ezekiel 14:3 there. Paul calls greed idolatry (Colossians 3:5), and 1 John 5:21 ends with a warning against idols. For the Hebrew word, see 8:10.

p: The written text has "in it"; the reading tradition has "he who comes". The Plain follows the reading tradition.
b: The consonants of this word are bh (Ketiv, "in it"), but the Masoretes marked the reading ba' (Qere, "he who comes"). The Plain follows the Qere because "in it" has no clear referent. Do not confuse it with 14:7, which has bi, "in my own person" ("I will answer him myself"). See the variant.

a: the foreigners who live in Israel
t: The resident foreigner under the same rule
p: Foreigners living in Israel are held to the same rule against idols, as in Leviticus 20:2.
b: The ger is a foreigner who lives among the Israelites, and the Torah usually puts him under the same laws as the native, especially the laws against idols and bloodshed (Leviticus 17:8-9; 20:2). Here he is covered by the same rule: if he brings idols into his heart and then consults the prophet, the LORD answers him the same way. The rule is not unfair to the foreigner; in 47:22-23 the same group receives a share of the land as if native-born. The Greek has "proselytes" (prosēlytoi), a word the later Jewish world used for converts.

a: it is I, the LORD, who enticed that prophet
p: A hard sentence. The verb patah can mean entice, persuade or deceive, and the readings differ on what God does.
b: Patah means "persuade, entice, deceive". The Plain says "enticed", as for the same verb in the lying spirit of 1 Kings 22:20-22 and in Jeremiah 20:7; English versions split between "deceived" (KJV, ESV) and "enticed" (NIV). The verb is passive in the first half ("is enticed") and active in the second ("I enticed"). The readings: (1) The LORD actively draws a prophet who has already chosen idols into error, as a judgment. The Greek in Swete's text has the first clause active ("if the prophet leads astray") and "I have led that prophet astray". Paul writes in a similar spirit of God giving people over to what they chose (Romans 1:24-28; 2 Thessalonians 2:11). (2) The LORD opens the door and lets the prophet follow his own wish. Rashi explains "I enticed" as "I opened a doorway for him to whatever he wishes", and adds that if a person wants to defile himself, they open the way for him (a saying he takes from Shabbat 104a). Radak compares the case of Ahab (1 Kings 22). In every reading the prophet is punished, not excused. See the cards below.

a: The guilt of the prophet will be the same
p: The one who asks for a lie and the one who gives it are equally guilty.
b: The rule is balanced: the prophet who deceives and the elder who asks with idols in his heart are judged alike. Jeremiah says that the people love to have it so: prophets prophesy falsely, priests rule by their own authority, and the people are glad of it (Jeremiah 5:31). Moses makes the same point for a prophet who calls Israel to other gods: the LORD is testing whether Israel loves him with all its heart (Deuteronomy 13:1-5). The people are not mere victims of false prophets; they asked.

p: Three famous righteous men. Ezekiel says their righteousness would save only themselves.
b: Noah was righteous in a wicked generation and saved his household in the ark (Genesis 6:9; 7:1). Job was "blameless and upright" (Job 1:1) and prayed for his friends (Job 42:8-9). The third, Daniel, is debated: the exile Daniel of the book of Daniel, who had saved the wise men of Babylon (Daniel 2:24), or an old righteous king Danel of the Ugaritic Tale of Aqhat who judged the cause of widows (a view set out in John Day's 1980 article). Jerome took him as the exile. Ezekiel's point is that even such men, famous for saving others, would save only themselves from a land under judgment. The sentence is built to be shocking: righteousness has a limit where guilt is great enough.
r: Genesis 6:9; Genesis 7:1; Job 1:1; Job 42:8-9; Daniel 2:24; Ezekiel 28:3; Jeremiah 15:1

p: Here the Hebrew is written without the usual yod. The reading tradition supplies it.
b: The consonants are dn'l, not dniyyel, the spelling of the book of Daniel. The written form (Ketiv) is Dan'el, while the reading tradition (Qere) says Daniyyel, which is the name of the exile in the book of Daniel. The unusual spelling is one reason some scholars connect this man with the Ugaritic Danel; others say a spelling cannot settle it. The Plain says "Daniel" in all three places.

p: Bread as the stick a person leans on; the phrase is from Leviticus 26:26. See the note at 4:16.
b: The same phrase appears at 4:16 and 5:16 (see the note at 4:16). Here it opens a case-by-case argument: when a land sins by "acting unfaithfully" (ma'al, the word for breaking faith with the LORD, used of Israel's betrayal of the covenant), the LORD may break its food supply, send wild animals, a sword or a plague. These are the curses of Leviticus 26:21-26 and Deuteronomy 28. The Plain uses "act unfaithfully" for ma'al everywhere, as in the Torah. Chapter 14 turns the list into a rule about who could stand in the gap, and answers: no one.
orig: מַטֵּה לֶחֶם (matteh lechem), מָעֲלָה מַעַל (ma'alah ma'al)

a: they would not save sons or daughters
t: No one saves a son or daughter
p: Even righteous people cannot rescue their children. Chapter 18 builds on this: each person answers for himself.
b: The oath "as I live" makes the rule certain. Abraham had bargained with God for Sodom, asking whether fifty, then ten righteous would spare the city (Genesis 18:23-32), and the LORD had told Jeremiah that even Moses and Samuel could not turn his heart toward this people (Jeremiah 15:1). Ezekiel goes further and says each righteous man would save only himself. This is the ground of chapter 18, where a son does not bear his father's guilt, nor a father his son's (18:20), and the LORD sets each person's life before him. It is not a rule against prayer: Ezekiel himself prayed (9:8; 11:13).

p: Sword, famine, wild animals and plague: a set from the curses of Leviticus 26 that returns in Revelation 6:8.
b: The four are the same list as the curse-chapter in Leviticus 26: wild beasts (26:22), sword (26:25), plague (26:25) and famine (26:26). Jeremiah 15:3 has four destroyers: sword, dogs, birds and wild animals. Ezekiel had already named three, sword, famine and plague (5:12, 17), and adds the fourth here, repeating each in 14:13-20. Revelation 6:8 says that death was given power over a fourth of the earth to kill with sword, famine, plague and wild animals. The words "how much worse" show Jerusalem's case: if even a single judgment would be enough to bring ruin on a land, all four on Jerusalem leave no hope.

p: The few who are brought to Babylon after 586 will show by their ways that the judgment was just.
b: The survivors who "come out to you" are those who will reach the exiles in Babylon after the city falls. Ezekiel learns of the fall from just such a survivor (33:21). Their conduct is not good; the exiles will see their "conduct and deeds" and see why the LORD judged. The comfort is not that the survivors are righteous but that the judgment has a reason ("not without cause"). This matches 12:16, where a few survive to tell of the abhorrent things, and 6:8-10, where the survivors will remember the LORD.

t: The vine: valued only for fruit
p: Israel is often called the LORD's vine. Here the question is what a vine is good for if it bears no fruit.
b: Israel is the LORD's vine in Isaiah 5:1-7, Psalm 80:8-16, Jeremiah 2:21 and Hosea 10:1. Those passages stress the vine's fruit and the owner's care. Ezekiel asks a different question: take away the fruit, and what is left? Vine wood is not like cedar or oak. It makes no beam, no tool and not even a peg to hang things on. A vine is worth only what it bears; when it bears nothing, it is fuel. The pride the exiles had in being the chosen vine is turned against them. Ezekiel returns to the vine in 17:5-10 and 19:10-14, and Jesus takes up the picture in John 15:1-6.

a: The fire has eaten away both ends
p: A stick already burned at both ends, and charred in the middle, is useless. Jerusalem had already been through fire.
b: A branch scorched at both ends and charred in the middle cannot be used for anything. The picture can fit what happened to Judah by 592 BC: the land had been ravaged, King Jehoiachin and thousands of its leading people had been taken in 597 BC (2 Kings 24:10-16), and what was left was half burned already. If it was useless when whole, it is more so now. The text does not say what the two ends are. Readers have suggested the northern kingdom (destroyed by Assyria in 722) and the first deportation of Judah; these are guesses, offered only as possible readings.

a: They have come out of the fire
t: Out of the fire, into the fire
p: Those who survived the first fall of Judah are not safe. The same fire comes again.
b: The people of Jerusalem have "come out of the fire": they survived the siege and deportation of 597 BC. They concluded that they were the ones the LORD had kept, and said the exiles were far from him (11:15). The oracle answers that surviving once proves nothing; the fire will consume them. This is why 15:6 speaks of "the people living in Jerusalem" and not of Israel as a whole. A similar thought is in Amos 4:11, where Israel is a brand plucked from a fire, but did not return to the LORD. Jerusalem did fall in 586 BC.

p: The word for breaking faith with the LORD, in the Torah and here.
b: Ma'al means to act unfaithfully, to betray a trust, especially by misusing what belongs to the LORD (Leviticus 5:15; Joshua 7:1). In Ezekiel it names Israel's whole history of idolatry and covenant-breaking (14:13; 17:20; 18:24; 20:27; 39:23, 26). The Plain says "act unfaithfully" every time, as in Leviticus and Chronicles, so that the reader can follow the word. The verse ends the vine parable by giving its charge: the land becomes a desolation because its people broke faith.
